FinanceTab.title: US lawmakers unveil bill to hold Wall Street’s ‘Epstein-connected’ bosses to account
FinanceTab.text:
US lawmakers have unveiled a new bill to hold Wall Street’s “Epstein-connected” bosses to account for helping finance the late sex offender’s crimes.

It came as top Democratic senator Elizabeth Warren condemned the UK bank Barclays for “dodging responsibility” over its failure to vet former boss Jes Staley and his ties to the once well-connected billionaire.

A bipartisan group of politicians, led by Warren and House representative Robert Garcia, are introducing a bill on Thursday known as the Epstein Wall Street Records Act. The bill follows a months-long investigation into the financier, who died in prison in 2019 while awaiting trial on child sex-trafficking charges.

If passed, the bill would force regulators including the Federal Reserve and the Securities and Exchange Commission to investigate “Epstein connected” financial firms and executives for potential breaches of banking, investment or illicit funding laws; and fine or even ban wrongdoers from the US financial sector.

The bill – which is also being backed by House Republican Thomas Massie – will also force regulators to publicly disclose any records relating to Epstein and his associates; and refer any potential criminal violations to the US justice department.

Warren said: “Since the big banks won’t hold themselves accountable – and the Trump administration won’t either – Congress must act to force real transparency and accountability for them and their executives who enabled Jeffrey Epstein’s crimes.”

News of the bill came as Warren condemned the bosses at Barclays, one of the UK’s biggest banks, over their failure to adequately answer questions about its former chief executives Jes Staley and his links to Epstein.

Staley’s ties with the well-connected billionaire spelled the end of his career. The American banker resigned from Barclays in November 2021, after UK regulators started investigating the true nature of his relationship with Epstein, whom he met in 2000 during his three-decade stint at JP Morgan.

The Financial Conduct Authority’s original investigation, triggered by a cache of more than 1,200 emails between Staley and Epstein, concluded that the pair were “indeed close” and had a relationship that “went beyond one that was professional in nature”.

Staley was eventually banned from the UK’s financial sector in 2023 for playing down those ties, and failed to overturn that decision in a court battle that revealed intimate details of the pair’s friendship last year.

That included Staley admitting to having sex with a member of Epstein’s staff in New York – an encounter he said was “consensual”. The case also revived a 2010 exchange referring to Disney princesses, in which Staley said: “That was fun. Say hi to Snow White.” Staley denied knowledge of the exchange during a UK court hearing.

After the loss of his legal challenge against the FCA, Staley said he was disappointed by the outcome but was “never dishonest”.

In July, Warren and a team of House Democrats wrote to the Barclays chair, Nigel Higgins, asking how it had vetted its former chief executive, and whether the bank had investigated potential “deficiencies” in its executive hiring process, given it had “allowed the board to hire a CEO who held extensive professional and personal ties to a convicted sex offender”.

Barclays has since responded with a letter from its head of US government relations, Lance Williams, that Warren said was not sufficient.

The letter focused on the findings of the UK regulators’ investigation. Williams stressed that Staley had “concealed information about his actions and the nature of his relationship with Mr Epstein” and only after Staley’s resignation had “previously unknown information come to light through various public disclosures”.

“This information paints a fundamentally different picture of Mr Staley than what he presented to Barclays,” Williams said, noting that Barclays had relied on external executive search firms to recruit Staley in 2015, when he was “known for his accomplishments in the banking industry”.

Warren said Barclays’ lacklustre response illustrated why it was time for regulators to launch formal investigations into Wall Street’s ties to Epstein: “Barclays continues to dodge responsibility over its apparent failure to vet its former CEO Jes Staley’s close professional and personal ties to Epstein.”

Barclays declined to comment. Staley’s legal representatives were contacted for comment.

FinanceTab.title: Tech market sell-off deepens amid fears over US inflation and AI debt
FinanceTab.text:
An accelerating sell-off of AI-linked shares has hit global markets, as fears over rising inflation and future interest rate hikes spooked traders already wary of the heavily indebted sector.

South Korea’s benchmark Kospi 200 index, which is heavily skewed towards the companies that make memory chips, fell more than 8% overnight to a six-month closing low, triggering circuit breakers that brought trading to a halt at various points.

Some of those semiconductor stocks, such as SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, plunged nearly 11% and 9.5% respectively. The index closed at a six-month low, down 8.1%.

Meanwhile, Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped by 4.9% on Thursday, after an 11% slump in the memory chip maker Kioxia and a 10% drop in SoftBank, a big investor in the ChatGPT owner, OpenAI.

The falls followed a slide on Wall Street during the previous day’s session, where the Nasdaq Composite fell by 1.9% and the S&P 500 dropped 1.1%, its worst performance since July.

US stocks fell further when trading resumed on Thursday. The Nasdaq dropped another 1.4% at the start of trading, with Dell, which makes datacentre servers, and Coherent, which manufactures components for AI datacentres, leading the early fallers.

The sell-off came after US data on Wednesday showed stateside inflation jumped to a higher-than-expected 3.7% in September, marking the fastest increase in prices since the consumer price index (CPI) rate hit a three-year peak of 4.2% in May.

Fresh data on Thursday showing US producers increased their prices by 6.3% year on year in September – the sharpest rise since December 2022 – added to inflationary jitters.

The figures have rattled investors who are now expecting fresh interest rate increases by the US Federal Reserve, with some punters pricing in another increase as soon as the end of the month.

“Markets have just had an incredibly tumultuous 24 hours, as a strong US CPI print was then followed up with mounting fears around the AI trade,” Deutsche Bank analysts led by Jim Reid said.

Worryingly, the figures showed this was not about fuel costs, which have been pushed up by geopolitical tensions including the ripple effects from the US war on Iran. Reid said: “This wasn’t just an energy surge driving prices higher, as there were broad-based moves across the consumer basket.”

The sell-off follows warnings from the International Monetary Fund, which said this week that the threat of an AI share price crash rippling out across global markets was putting world financial stability at risk.

“The consequences of an AI correction could be global,” the IMF said. Aside from the US, Asian markets would be most exposed, with the UK and eurozone potentially more insulated – although investors with US holdings would be hit.

The latest jitters hit China, where the Shanghai Shenzhen CSI 300 slipped by as much as 2.4%, marking the lowest level since August 2025. In Taiwan, one of the world’s leading chip makers and Asia’s most valuable company, TSMC, fell 2% despite reporting its sixth straight quarter of profits.

European stocks also came under pressure, with Germany’s DAX down 0.36% in afternoon trading and the Italian FTSE MIB dropping by 1.3%.

FinanceTab.title: US inflation rose to 3.7% in September in blow to Republicans before midterms
FinanceTab.text:
Republicans are entering the midterm elections with the highest rate of inflation since the spring, according to a government report released on Wednesday.

US price increases reached an annual rate of 3.7% in September, according to the latest data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, up from 3.4% in August. This final inflation report before the pivotal midterm elections comes amid polls showing widespread dissatisfaction with the Trump administration over the cost of living.

Price increases are the highest they have been since the annual inflation rate reached a three-year peak of 4.2% in May. Gasoline accounted for over half of overall price increases, up 34% from last year. Fuel oil, which is used to heat homes, increased by 74% from last year, a worrying sign for households heading into the winter. Air travel, which many Americans rely on during the holidays, also increased by 22.4%.

Overall, consumer prices went up 0.6% from August. Core inflation, which strips out volatile energy and food prices, also ticked up by 0.3% in September to 2.6% annually.

Price increases this year have largely driven by the US-Israel war with Iran, which has caused energy prices to soar. Average gas prices remain over a dollar per gallon more than last year, according to data from AAA. Meanwhile diesel, which powers domestic supply chains, reached a record high last month.

September’s inflation rate is the highest it has been before a midterm election, with the exception of the pandemic, since 1990.

The economy has consistently been cited as a top issue for American voters, as rising gasoline prices and persistent inflation have eaten into household budgets. Higher energy prices from the Iran war have cost Americans more than $1,020 per household, according to Brown University, and a total of $133bn for all US consumers.

Much of the anger is expected to be directed at Republicans, who control Congress and the White House. According to a recent survey from Reuters/Ipsos, 78% of Americans blame the current Trump administration’s policies for inflation that is outpacing their earnings, including 57% of Republicans who support Donald Trump.

In recent weeks, Trump has attempted to downplay his administration’s role in price increases, pointing to the Iranian government as the cause of the squeeze. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the latest inflation report.

On Tuesday, Trump posted on social media that Yemen’s Houthi group was attacking Saudi Arabia in a deliberate effort to affect the upcoming elections.

“They’ve emerged again, probably at the behest of Iran … in a very nasty way, hitting Saudi Arabia, and purposefully trying to drive up Oil Prices, probably prior to the U.S. Elections — NOT NICE,” he wrote.

Later on Tuesday, Trump defended his record on the economy during a rally in Wasilla, Alaska, saying that his support for families has been “substantial”. “Every time they want to try and get me, they say ‘affordability’,” he said.

Heightened inflation will put more pressure on the Federal Reserve to increase interest rates, its tool to cool prices. Last month, the Fed raised interest rates for the first time since 2023, citing elevated prices. Higher rates affect the cost of borrowing money, including mortgage rates. The 30-year mortgage rate, applied to the most commonly used loans for home ownership, is up to 7.40%.

SportsTab.title: Gianni Infantino: Fifa president apologises over World Cup move but told he must do more
SportsTab.text:
President Gianni Infantino has apologised to the Fifa Council for his World Cup sell-off plan - but has been told he is not fit to lead unless he releases all the documents and answers key questions.

The Fifa Council met in Zurich on Thursday for the first time since Infantino's secret Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal emerged.

Under FFE, which Infantino scrapped within days, a portion of the commercial rights of football's world governing body would have been given to a private investment firm.

In a three-and-a-half-hour meeting, Infantino also faced questions about US striker Folarin Balogun's suspended red-card ban, the Fifa Peace Prize and funding for national associations.

Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt - a Fifa vice-president - said afterwards that many questions remained unanswered despite the "most robust, most frank, most open Council meeting" she had experienced.

"One of the disappointing things is that we didn't get answers to anything that we had specifically requested - for example getting the papers from FFE," Hewitt said.

"I asked the question 'why not?' - and we were asked to submit those questions in writing.

"I think the man has to answer those questions and if he doesn't answer those questions now, he's not fit to be Fifa president - and that was what was shared in the meeting."

Hewitt added: "I've repeatedly asked for the papers to be shared. I haven't received them and still in spite of the request today, I haven't received them.

"It is the rationale for why FFE happened in the way that it did, the Balogun case, the Peace Prize.

"The responses to those questions, which I still don't have answers to, will determine from my personal point of view whether or not Gianni is the right candidate.

"That will be the point at which or not we can say that any individual that was involved in FFE can or cannot be trusted because until we see what actually happened it's very difficult to say behaviour needs or not to change."

Hewitt acknowledged there had been "some contrition" in Infantino's apology.

"Then there were no holds barred in terms of what we felt about what had happened," she added.

"What he really apologised for was not bringing it to the Council. If you regret it that deeply, share it with us."

Uefa - European football's governing body - has been one of Infantino's fiercest critics and has repeatedly called on him to stand down.

It has prepared criminal legal proceedings against Infantino and lodged a claim in three US courts for all documents related to FFE to be released.

Hewitt hopes Infantino now freely releases the documents so the Council can understand what happened.

"Those papers coming to Council are a crucial next part of us feeling comfortable as to what, if any, criminal proceedings need to take place," Hewitt said.

Asked if there was any change in stance from Uefa about Infantino, she added: "From my position, nothing has shifted. I've no new information that makes me feel any differently, other than we do have a president who is apologetic."

Infantino will stand for re-election as Fifa president for a third time in March, and as yet no credible candidate has emerged to challenge the Swiss-Italian.

Former Tottenham and Switzerland defender Ramon Vega has said he intends to run, but it appears unlikely he will get the five letters of support from member associations let alone be a serious contender.

Senior figures within European football have told BBC Sport they want former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger to run.

But it is unclear whether Wenger would be prepared to give up his position as Fifa's global head of football development for a fight against his boss that he may not win.

Hewitt accepted Uefa - and Infantino's other opponents around the world - must find someone to put their name on the ballot before the deadline of 18 November.

She also indicated it would be important for the president to have a rival after being re-elected unopposed in 2019 and 2023.

"I think it's important to Gianni to have somebody who stands with a different manifesto, and good for Fifa to have that choice," Hewitt added.

"We're in a democracy here. We must remember there are 211 associations and it's really important that all 211 associations have the opportunity to vote according to how they feel.

"This is somebody first and foremost who puts football first right at the heart of everything that they do. Secondly, it has to be somebody who unites the world. Thirdly, somebody who needs to have the courage to bring about reforms."

Hewitt said Balogun avoiding a suspension after being sent off at the World Cup was one of the "biggest issues".

Balogun's ban was suspended after US President Donald Trump asked for the decision to be reviewed.

BBC Sport understands a proposal was put to the Council to amend the Fifa disciplinary code, which would prevent a repeat.

Under that, regulations would be amended to state the disciplinary committee could not suspend an automatic one-match ban for a red card.

"What happened in July did not serve football... whether it's the Balogun case, the FFE case... the reputation of football was put under serious threat," said Hewitt.

"Once behaviour starts to influence what happens on the pitch, then I think it's a dark day for football and a number of people said that in the room."

The Fifa Peace Prize - awarded to President Trump - was also raised, but Hewitt said Infantino's behaviour with "other maybe celebrities and dignitaries" was also discussed.

"When he puts other dignitaries in front of his 211 associations, then he's lost what football is about," Hewitt said.

"And that was said by a number of people, not just the Europeans."

How the Peace Prize came to be awarded will be the subject of an investigation by the Fifa social committee.

"They will consider, first of all, how the Peace Prize came about, whether it should have come about, whether it should have been awarded in the way that it was, who made that decision and whether or not it should be taken out or whether it should be reformed," Hewitt said.

"That committee will report back to Council in December and then Council will make the decision based on its recommendation.

"Today there was a watershed moment where it's very clear in order to move forward, which we all want to do, we have to understand the past."

SportsTab.title: Rugby League World Cup 2026: Reece Walsh vomits and Kalyn Ponga plays through pain
SportsTab.text:
If anyone doubted the physical commitment of rugby league's greatest stars, they only needed to watch an exhausted Reece Walsh doubled up and vomiting during Thursday's epic World Cup opener between Australia and New Zealand.

And during the Kangaroos' dramatic 24-22 victory in Sydney, there were plenty of other examples of that commitment - aside from the normal rough and tumble this punishing sport regularly delivers.

New Zealand full-back Kalyn Ponga bravely battled on for 20 minutes with a suspected broken arm before almost having to be scraped off the pitch minutes before hat-trick hero Jack Bostock's winning try for the Kangaroos.

Mitchell Moses initially tried to run off a calf issue before being forced from the field just after the break, while Australia captain Isaah Yeo demonstrated his durability against a powerhouse Kiwis pack, having elected to delay surgery on his injured pectoral muscle just in order play in the tournament.

But understandably, much of the focus was on the star full-backs - Ponga and Walsh.

The Kangaroos number one was playing for the first time for eight weeks after recovering from an ankle injury.

And he delivered a superb try-saving tackle on Ponga during the first-half before scoring a with a sensational 60-metre burst to lay the platform for the Kangaroos' last-gasp victory.

"Walshy was very good tonight having not played for eight weeks," said Australia head coach Kevin Walters.

"I thought he was really good. That try-saving tackle he did is equal to anything that he can do an attack, and then he comes up with a couple of big plays in attack as well.

"He's cramping and vomiting and all sorts of things. He didn't have the energy to kick the goal. He's a chucker [he throws up]. People get nicknames and his nickname is 'Chucker'.

"He's not an endurance athlete. He's a power athlete and he had some big efforts there a couple of times, back-to-back and we've seen him do that before."

Yeo added: "For Reece to come back in a contest like that with some of those plays is a massive effort after not playing for eight weeks. It won't get spoken about enough but it is really hard to do at this level.

"He has just got the ability to just make people miss. I think he made two people miss on the one move but he's just one of those players that can just break a game open, and we probably needed that."

SportsTab.title: Lisandro Martinez: Roy Keane says Man Utd 'like a circus'
SportsTab.text:
Former captain Roy Keane says Manchester United are "like a circus" after defender Lisandro Martinez criticised the club's hierarchy.

Speaking after Tuesday's 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid in the Champions League, Martinez said he had expected more investment in the squad in the summer and "more from our technical director".

In a social media post on Wednesday he said he had spoken out of "anger and frustration".

The loss in Madrid stretched United's winless run to five games, and they have won just one of their opening six matches of the Premier League season.

Keane, speaking on The Overlap, external podcast, said Martinez's statement reflected the overall state of the club.

"There will be some fans saying it's great and some saying you're letting the team down, especially from a player who hasn't been at his best, when the team is struggling," he said.

"I think as a reflection of the club, it's obviously chaos there, like a bit of a circus.

"When you're going through a difficult spell like United are, the issue I have with certain players saying things is you always have to start with the man in the mirror before you start coming out with all these comments."

SportsTab.title: Formula 1: The pit stop that helped save lives
SportsTab.text:
When the McLaren pit crew refuelled a car, changed its tyres and relayed information to their driver in less than seven seconds at the Spanish Grand Prix in 2001, they were just doing their jobs.

But 700 miles away in the break room at Great Ormond Street Hospital (GOSH), Dr Martin Elliott and his colleagues were watching after completing a life-saving operation on a young child.

The brief glimpse would change how the doctors approached patient care. From surgery-to-ICU handovers and neonatal care to air-ambulance response times, F1's innovations have made an impact far beyond the track.

At Ferrari's factory in Maranello, the GOSH medical team studied how pit crews organised roles, communication and handovers.

Doctors and nurses started each procedure with a checklist, setting out specific roles and tasks. This reduced human error and helped ensure key tasks were completed. All patient data was also shared from the operating theatre to the care unit.

Gaps in performance were identified and addressed, while repeated rehearsals helped refine the process.

As a result, the process from surgery to intensive care became more organised, and a 2007 study by researchers at GOSH and the University of Oxford found the F1-inspired handover process reduced technical errors, information omissions and handover time.

Reflecting on the project, Dr Elliott, then a consultant paediatric cardiothoracic surgeon at GOSH, said: "The environment we were working in then and in many ways still do is fundamentally potentially dangerous at every step.

"And of course, fundamentally, that's how F1 doesn't make mistakes. They have created an environment of complete precision, not only in engineering, but also in process, because they simply can't afford financially or from a race perspective to slip up.

"It's the same, you know, the precious parcel on the trolley is the same as the precious parcel in the car. You have to get all of those steps right."

The model was later adopted by other healthcare teams.

SportsTab.title: Wuhan Open: Sonay Kartal beats Jasmine Paolini to reach quarter-finals
SportsTab.text:
Britain's Sonay Kartal continued her impressive comeback from long-term injury with a comfortable win over former Wimbledon finalist Jasmine Paolini to reach the Wuhan Open quarter-finals.

Kartal, 24, missed more than six months with a stress fracture in her back, but has won five of her seven matches since returning to action.

The former world number 44 ruthlessly brushed aside Italian 15th seed Paolini 6-2 6-0 with a performance that further validated Kartal's patient approach to recovering from the first serious injury of her career.

It was another statement performance from Karta following her straight-set win over ninth seed Belinda Bencic in the previous round.

"Against someone as good as Jasmine is, I knew I had to be solid from the start and not let up," Kartal said.

"From my side, it was a pretty flawless performance."

Kartal was riding the crest of a wave in the early part of the season, having broken into the world's top 50, reached two WTA quarter-finals and recorded wins over top-class opponents.

Victories over 2025 Australian Open champion Madison Keys and former world number eight Emma Navarro in Indian Wells led to a meeting with now world number one Elena Rybakina in the fourth round.

However, Kartal was forced to retire with a back injury that proved more serious than first thought.

After initially hoping she would make a quick recovery, Kartal was left unable to brush her teeth without "being in agony", leading to some difficult decisions.

Missing Wimbledon was a particularly tough choice, especially given she reached the fourth round of her home Grand Slam in 2025, but resigning herself to not rushing a comeback has proved wise.

Her first match back a little over three weeks ago - representing Great Britain at the BJK Cup - ended in a narrow defeat, before she won two matches to reach the Beijing third round in her WTA Tour return.

"At the BJK Cup, the level I produced was much higher than I thought and I left super happy," Kartal said.

"Now I'm growing in confidence with every match I'm playing."

SportsTab.title: Fifa: Could Arsene Wenger take on Gianni Infantino for presidency?
SportsTab.text:
Despite the backlash caused by his failed plan to sell commercial stakes in the World Cup to private investors, Fifa president Gianni Infantino looks increasingly likely to be re-elected unopposed for a fourth and final term next year.

But could there be a sensational twist?

Senior figures within European football have told BBC Sport they want former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger to run as a surprise candidate.

But would the man who has been the governing body's head of global development since 2019 really challenge his own boss? And what lies behind the support he has?

On Thursday the Fifa Council will meet for the first time since the emergence of Infantino's Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme plunged the organisation into crisis, leading to calls from the game's leaders in Europe, North America and Asia for him to step down.

A defiant Infantino will come face to face with some of his fiercest critics at what could be a spicy gathering in Zurich.

Fifa is set to propose a $3.4bn (£2.6bn) increase in the amount of money it hands out for football development. But Infantino will also face scrutiny over governance reforms, FFE, the awarding of the inaugural Fifa Peace Prize last year to US President Donald Trump, and disciplinary procedures in the wake of the Folarin Balogun affair.

But the meeting will also bring into sharp focus the failure so far to identify a unifying figure with the worldwide appeal to challenge Infantino.

While potential rivals like Victor Montagliani, the president of the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football (Concacaf), and Uefa chief Aleksander Ceferin have let it be known they are not contenders, Infantino has been busy touring the world, shoring up his position.

The growing expectation is that such is the support he retains in his power base of Africa, South America and Oceania, he will be returned, despite only carrying the backing of roughly half of Fifa's 211 members.

To date, the only person to declare their intention to run is the former Tottenham defender Ramon Vega, although few rate his chances.

So could Wenger be the answer?

Here in Zurich, there is no indication that he is plotting a bid. On Wednesday evening Wenger joined Infantino and other Fifa Council members for dinner in a Zurich restaurant. As a senior member of Fifa's management team, he will also be present at Thursday's meeting.

When BBC Sport asked about his intentions via Fifa, no comment was provided.

Meanwhile, those close to the 76 year-old, who left Arsenal in 2018 after 22 years in which he became the most successful manager in the club's history, will not be drawn on whether he is interested.

One told BBC Sport he would be "an ideal candidate, but he is his own man".

What is clear is that he does have supporters, who believe he commands the level of respect beyond Europe that would be essential if the Uefa-led rebellion against Infantino is to have any chance of success.

"He isn't a football politician, but it would bring football and integrity to the leadership of Fifa" says Alex Phillips, a former Uefa and Fifa executive told the BBC.

"It's become way too much focused on money and not enough focused on football. And I think someone like that would put football back as the main priority. Let's see what he decides. There may be other candidates as well."

A current senior official at a European national association agrees that Wenger "truly understands football development because he's been running it.

"People don't see him as just a European. He's very respected in Asia, for instance, from his time working in Japan. A lot of people are saying he'd be the ideal candidate. With him, it's not about money, status or ego. He genuinely loves the game.

"He's made a difficult role work and understands Fifa, and that's why he'd be a really good candidate.

"That said, he's in a really difficult position."

That was highlighted amid the fallout over FFE, when Wenger, who has traditionally been loyal to Infantino, distanced himself from the aborted plot.

"I was not involved in this strategic plan and first became aware of the project through media reports," Wenger said in a statement at the time. "The decision to withdraw the project was absolutely necessary and beyond question, because I firmly believe in an independent Fifa that serves our game with commitment, transparency and integrity."

Some may have expected Wenger to resign over the controversy, given his thinly veiled criticism of Infantino, the way he had been kept in the dark, and the condemnation of the plot from stakeholders across the game. But he has carried on in a role in which he oversees youth development at academies in 60 countries, as well as youth competitions around the world. He is also a technical adviser to rule-making body International Football Association Board (Ifab).

Wenger has caused controversy at times in his Fifa role, notably for proposals such as biennial World Cups, and the idea of a 'daylight' offside law.

But he also has a global profile, including in Africa, where Infantino recently received a major re-election boost when receiving the backing of all 54 member national associations after promising an increase in funding.

Known as a champion of African players when in charge at Arsenal, Wenger's support of an expanded 48-team World Cup in order to drive development in countries beyond the game's traditional powers has been well received in the continent.

Indeed, at the weekend Wenger was in Cape Verde at a Confederation of African Football conference, telling the delegates: "We want to see an African team win the World Cup, and the numbers show that it is feasible."

Such sentiments would do him no harm if he was to stand for president.

BBC Sport has been told that a large number of Fifa's staff also want Wenger to run, and believe he could change the organisation's image.

Others, however, are more sceptical. One well-connected figure in Fifa circles told BBC Sport that he would be "amazed if Wenger would rise up against the man who appointed him in the first place. Arsene has had some fairly 'out there' ideas. In terms of the administration of the game and the relationships on a political level, in the kind of places you're going to need to corral and command power, I'm not sure he's the man for that."

Another senior European official said: "He has the stature, but I'm not sure he smacks of the future. Maybe he could do a single term to introduce reforms. He is very respected in the game and has done a good job of the development programmes, but whether he'd split from Gianni, I just don't know."

If Wenger does want to run, he has until 18 November to declare his candidacy, and would need to be nominated by at least five national associations.

As a manager, Wenger is remembered as a legendary figure who changed English football with his forward-thinking approach to tactics and nutrition.

Could he attempt a shake-up of a different kind at Fifa? It is an intriguing prospect.

SportsTab.title: Rafael Camara: Haas sign Brazilian for F1 debut in 2027 season
SportsTab.text:
Brazilian Rafael Camara will join the US-based Haas team for his debut Formula 1 season in 2027.

The 21-year-old, who is leading the Formula 2 championship, has been chosen after a selection process including a total of four drivers.

Camara was picked over the reigning F2 champion Leonardo Fornaroli and Haas reserve drivers Jack Doohan and Ryo Hirakawa after they were assessed in tests in previous years' F1 cars.

Camara, Fornaroli and Hirakawa were all assessed at a test at Portugal's Portimao track in August, Doohan separately.

Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu said that Camara had been the quickest driver at the tests.

"I always said we would choose driver by performance. He showed incredible speed. That was the fully overriding factor above everything else," Komatsu said.

"In Portimao, he was just simply outstanding. We really wanted to go for someone who had that natural speed.

"He showed that he could handle himself very well with not a huge amount of time to learn the car. He showed us more than just raw speed."

Komatsu added that all the drivers tested came with financial backing, adding: "But it was clear he was the quickest guy, so we took him purely based on that."

Haas have not said who will race their other car next season, but it is considered only a matter of time before Briton Oliver Bearman is confirmed in the seat for a third season.

Komatsu said: "It is our intention to continue with Ollie. It is just a matter of timing and finalising certain details."

Bearman and Camara are both members of the Ferrari driver academy.

Frenchman Esteban Ocon will leave the team at the end of the year after two seasons alongside Bearman, Haas confirmed at the end of last month.

Camara said: "It's an important step in my career and I want to thank (owner) Gene Haas and Ayao Komatsu for the trust they have placed in me.

"Now my focus is on preparing myself in the best possible way for this new challenge.

"There will be a lot to learn, and I'm looking forward to working closely with the team, understanding the car and continuing to develop as a driver."

SportsTab.title: South Africa vs Australia: Low Test crowds prompt review
SportsTab.text:
A senior South African cricket official has pledged to order a review into the low crowd which attended the first Test against Australia in Durban.

Despite South Africa being the reigning world Test champions and Australia the number one-ranked side in the world, less than 20,000 fans attended across the five days.

Australia, who are touring South Africa for the first time since the 2018 sandpaper scandal, won by 214 runs and can wrap up the three-match series when the second Test gets under way in Gqeberha on Sunday.

"It is impossible to overlook our disappointment that just under 20,000 fans attended across the five days," said KwaZulu-Natal Cricket Union chief executive Heinrich Strydom.

"A Test match of this quality deserved greater support in the stands. This is something we will reflect on through a thorough internal review.

"We need to listen to our supporters, reconnect with our communities and continue to find ways to make Test cricket more accessible, engaging and appealing.

"Test cricket is part of our sporting heritage and its future depends on all of us."

Attendances for Test cricket have been declining in many places around the world, most notably in South Africa and the West Indies.

However, live sport does remain a big draw in South Africa.

While the Test against Australia was ongoing, a football cup final between Orlando Pirates and Mamelodi Sundowns was being held across town in Durban which attracted more than 50,000 fans.

"While we recognise supporters face competing demands on their time and finances, we must also understand better what influences their decisions to attend and what more we can do to make live cricket an attractive and worthwhile experience," added Strydom.

On the pitch, South Africa have responded to their heavy first-Test defeat by calling up "Aussie agitator" Matthew Breetzke.

Batter Breetzke has been added to the squad at the expense of Tristan Stubbs, who is left out for the second Test after making scores of 32 and one in Durban.

Wicketkeeper Kyle Verreynne remains in the squad but loses the gloves, with Ryan Rickelton in line to keep wicket. Breetzke and the uncapped Marques Ackerman look set to come into the top order in place of Stubbs and Verreynne.

Earlier in the tour, Breetzke made a century in the first one-day international but drew the ire of the Australians when he pinched a single after a throw rebounded off his body.

Cricket Australia's own website said the 27-year-old "got under Australia's skin" and described him as an "Aussie agitator", while South Africa coach Shukri Conrad admitted Breetzke's temperament was a factor in his inclusion.

"The attitude and character that Matt brings and has, I think that will go a long way," said Conrad.

Breetzke has played two previous Tests, managing only 14 runs in three innings, and has not played a first-class match since February.

However, the right-hander has made a sublime start to his one-day international career, averaging almost 59 from 17 matches.

South Africa must avoid defeat in the second Test, starting on Sunday, to avoid losing the three-match series with a game to spare.

The 214-run loss in the first Test was the world champions' first defeat in captain Temba Bavuma's 13 matches in charge.

The hosts look likely to include attack leader Kagiso Rabada after the pace bowler missed the first Test as part of his recovery from a hamstring injury.

Australia will have their own decisions to make over the batting line-up after being forced into changes for the first Test.

Injuries to Cameron Green and Josh Inglis meant a first Test in 10 years for Nic Maddinson. The opener was called into the XI despite not playing a first-class game in the previous 19 months following treatment for testicular cancer.

With Maddinson at the top of the order, Matthew Renshaw shuffled down to number five and produced a career-best performance. The Middlesbrough-born left-hander made scores of 190 and 82, as well as claiming two wickets with his off-breaks.

Australia head coach Andrew McDonald said Green is "progressing well" from an abdominal injury, while Inglis has started batting again after suffering a broken finger.

If either or both are passed fit, it would possibly mean Maddinson sits out, with Renshaw once again pushed up to open.

SportsTab.title: Vinicius Junior: From contract uncertainty to conspiracy theories and a four-match ban
SportsTab.text:
A bizarre online rumour, a red card and a four-match suspension have put Vinicius Jr back into the spotlight at a crucial point in Real Madrid's season.

First, over the summer, came the uncertainty over his future at Real Madrid, with contract talks stalling for more than 18 months and Arsenal reportedly among the clubs interested in the Brazilian.

Those negotiations eventually reached a resolution, with Vinicius securing an improved deal, but the headlines have continued.

Then came bizarre conspiracy theories claiming he had been replaced by a body double, following cosmetic surgery he had done after the World Cup.

Now, following his dismissal against Villarreal at the weekend, a four-match suspension means he is ruled out of El Clasico against Barcelona a week on Sunday.

But beyond the social media frenzy and disciplinary controversy, bigger questions are emerging about Vinicius' form, his on-pitch behaviour and his relationship with the Real Madrid supporters.

A key moment was when Jose Mourinho opted to start the Brazilian on the bench for the match against Villarreal, their first since the international break.

It was the first time since last April that Vinicius had not started a match for the club, with Mourinho handing Yan Diomande a place in the starting XI instead.

"What makes me sad is the fact he really wants to be at his absolute best," Mourinho said beforehand.

"He wants to be the Vini who wins games, scores goals and makes the difference. Seeing the pain he feels himself makes me sad. He is an extraordinary guy who works very hard to get back to his absolute best.

"He deserves better treatment, as he has made Madrid very happy on many occasions."

Vinicius has been continually booed and whistled by some Real Madrid supporters this season, along with other players.

After entering the game in the 52nd minute he looked to have made an immediate impact, scoring what Real believed to be their second goal after a Jude Bellingham assist.

Vinicius raced towards the supporters, kissing the badge before being engulfed by his team-mates, who piled on top of him in celebration.

Even Mourinho sprinted across the pitch to join the celebrations, which felt like a public display of his faith in the Brazilian.

A VAR review changed everything.

The referee was sent to the monitor, which showed Vinicius pulling Nathan Saliba's hair while the ball was in play and neither player was challenging for it.

The referee overturned the goal and instead showed Vinicius a straight red card.

The Brazilian's reaction to the decision then became a further disciplinary issue, with team-mates having to intervene as he continued to protest.

Mourinho refused to speak to press afterwards. News travelled around the media room that Mourinho felt if he did speak, he would say something that would get him suspended.

Two hours before Real faced Roma in the Champions League on Wednesday, the Spanish football federation's disciplinary committee handed Vinicius a four-match suspension.

Two matches were imposed for the hair-pulling incident, with a further two for his protests following the dismissal.

The punishment rules him out of league fixtures against Sevilla, Barcelona, Racing Santander and Valencia. Most significantly, it means he will miss El Clasico, unless an appeal changes the outcome.

Mourinho expressed his frustration at the timing of the announcement, questioning why it came just two hours before their Champions League match.

"Do you think it's normal for a player who is going to play an important match for Spanish football to know two hours before that he is sanctioned with four games? You don't need to answer me," Mourinho said.

"It's not normal. Couldn't they do it now or tomorrow morning? We found out on the bus and almost arrived at the stadium."

The Portuguese coach described the decision as showing "little respect" for the club and suggested the timing was intentional, particularly with Madrid facing a demanding schedule in the coming days.

Following Real Madrid's 4-3 victory over Roma, Vinicius also addressed the incident, having apologised to his team and fans on social media.

"I don't remember any player ever getting a four-game suspension," Vinicius said. "I tried to get past the player in front of me and ended up grabbing his hair.

"That's it – a red card. That's why I was so surprised, but I didn't say a single bad word to the referee to deserve a four-game suspension."

The forward also acknowledged his frustration at being substituted in the 59th minute against Roma when Real Madrid were trailing 3-1. They then scored three late goals to stage a remarkable comeback win.

"It's normal for me to get upset after being substituted because I always want to play every match," he said.

"I'm aware of my form and how I'm playing. I'm here to help the team, and sometimes I need to come off so other players can play and change the dynamics."

The Brazilian has gone six appearances for Real Madrid without scoring, with his last goal coming in August against Real Sociedad.

The 26-year-old has also become the subject of bizarre conspiracy theories on social media after undergoing a cosmetic surgery procedure on his chin in July.

Because of the visible differences, rumours on social media suggested Vinicius had been replaced by a body double.

Meanwhile, Vinícius's personal life has also made headlines in Brazil, with his reported split from Brazilian-American television personality Virginia Fonseca dominating coverage over the weekend.

The internet may continue searching for extraordinary explanations on why Vinicius has experienced a dip in form, but Real Madrid need to find answers on the pitch.

The win against Roma, especially coming from two goals down, was described by Vinicius as a "huge boost for the team".

He assured fans that he will be back to his best form as soon as possible.

"I know I'm not at my best right now, but I've had worse moments, and even when people doubted me, I've always stood up for this club," he said.

"That's why I renewed for six more years. The good streak will return, and the goals will come back. I'm sure of that. I have no doubt. I'm here to help the team."

SportsTab.title: Rugby World Cup 2035: Spain bids to host tournament and use Nou Camp and Bernabeu
SportsTab.text:
Barcelona's Nou Camp, Real Madrid's Bernabeu and the Mestalla in Valencia are all on a list of possible stadiums as Spain bids to host the Rugby World Cup in 2035.

The Spanish Rugby Federation says it aims to deliver the "best World Cup in history", connecting the tournament to 700 million Spanish speakers worldwide.

If Spain's bid is successful, the revamped Nou Camp is in line to host the final, which would be the first time the World Cup showpiece has been held in front of more than 100,000 fans.

Argentina and Japan are also bidding to host the tournament, with World Rugby expected to announce its preferred bidder in the spring or summer of 2027.

Spanish rugby authorities say the tournament in 2035 would capitalise on the Fifa World Cup in 2030, with Spain joint hosts along with Morocco and Portugal.

The Rugby World Cup bid has the support of the Spanish government as well as La Liga, with some of the most iconic stadiums in world football on a list of potential venues.

"We have complete confidence in our organisational capability, our sports infrastructure is at the cutting edge of innovation, and we are convinced that hosting Rugby World Cup 2035 will bring new and unique dimensions of hospitality, collaboration, unity and friendship to the global rugby family," said Juan Carlos Martin 'Hansen', executive president of the Spanish federation.

Spain have qualified for the 2027 tournament in Australia, which will be their first appearance at a men's World Cup since 1999.

The Spanish federation has an ambition to triple the number of people playing the sport in the country by 2035 and, ultimately, establish Spain as a Tier One rugby nation.

"Rugby is becoming part of our country's identity," added Martin.

"Working together with World Rugby, we can make Rugby World Cup 2035 a turning point in the global growth of the sport, for the benefit of generations to come."

Seven-time participants in the Women's Rugby World Cup, Spain has hosted two European finals weekends - at Bilbao's San Mames in 2018 and 2026 - while the 2016 Top 14 final was held at the Nou Camp in front of 99,124 supporters.

The San Mames is on a list of 14 stadiums submitted to World Rugby, which will be reduced to 9 or 10 if the Spanish bid is successful.

Spain has also staged World Rugby Sevens events, with further editions confirmed in Castile and Leon for 2027 and 2028 respectively.

SportsTab.title: Bueckers broadsides to Lady Magic’s spice: the greatest trash talkers in WNBA history
SportsTab.text:
Today, even the most casual of WNBA fans have watched some of the league’s biggest stars talking trash on the court. But while the snarling convos look heated, most of the time, they are good-natured, competitive fun.

Still, we wondered, who are the best trash talkers in the game? Which players over the years have turned talking smack into an art form? Let’s explore.

OK, Miller never played in the league – she retired before the W’s launch in 1997 – but if there was a trash-talking trophy in the WNBA, it would have to be named after her. Miller is considered by many to be the best women’s basketball player of all time (she once scored 105 points in a high school game), and those who saw her at USC or heard her in the booth on TNT know that she can really talk. Of course, her talent for it began in the back yard playing against her younger brother, fellow Hall of Famer Reggie Miller. From there, a legend was made.

Another candidate for greatest player of all time and, like Miller, Taurasi had a knack for talking smack. She did it both on and off the court. For example, in 2016, when the men’s and women’s US basketball teams were together on a cruise ship, Taurasi yelled over to an already-blustery Draymond Green, “Hey, Draymond, how does it feel to be the only person in this room who’s never been double-teamed?” Taurasi doesn’t mind – she’ll even go after the league’s biggest names, chirping incessantly in the ears of players like Caitlin Clark.

Angel Reese/Caitlin Clark

Like Larry Bird and Magic Johnson, these two players will for ever be linked. It all began in college in the NCAA Tournament when Reese talked some legendary trash to Clark, pointing at her finger as if to say, “Where’s your championship ring?” Those images made global headlines. Since then, the two have been rivals. (Even the famed former Showtime point guard has noticed.) “They jaw at each other,” offered Las Vegas Aces coach Becky Hammon. But their trash talking isn’t only reserved for each other. Clark is willing to talk smack to anyone after a big shot and Reese is on the brink of a title – something she predicted loudly last year. But despite all their verbal battles, Reese and Clark, like Bird and Magic, seem to be more than amicable off the floor these days.

In a poll by the Athletic last year, Thomas was voted by her peers as the biggest and best trash talker in the league. That’s saying something, but Thomas wears the crown proudly. Explained one opponent: “She smiles and talks shit, that’s the crazy part, it’s psycho stuff, she’s crazy, man.” Said another: “Everyone knows AT talks shit. I don’t even guard her, and she talks shit to me.” Certainly, Thomas is not one to back down from anything. She was even fined and suspended earlier this year for throwing an elbow at Clark. While that isn’t exactly verbal communication, Thomas did send a message.

Drafted just last year, Bueckers has quickly become one of the WNBA’s best. She’s an assassin on the floor, capable of hitting game-winner after game-winner. And she’ll let you know about it, too. She’ll strike even if you’re on the bench, before nailing a three. Whether she’s speaking up for fellow players or talking smack to her opponent after a hard foul, Bueckers is not someone to mess with. “I don’t really start it,” she told Jennifer Hudson, with a smile, “but if somebody gets me going …” Yes, that would be a bad idea.

Lieberman is one of the legends of the women’s game. Known in her heyday as “Lady Magic” for her skill at point guard, she was also one of the most biting trash talkers, according to her former GM with the Women’s Professional Basketball League’s Dallas Diamonds, Nancy Nichols. “From my experience, Nancy Lieberman was pretty spicy!” Nichols tells the Guardian. “Especially when she played street ball with the Washington Generals on the Harlem Globetrotters’ tour.” That’s right: Lieberman was so good that she was a standout in the men’s and women’s game. More recently, though, when former NBA All-Star Jeff Teague criticized Lieberman’s friend and mentee Clark, Lieberman came to the Fever star’s defense, telling Teague, “Jeff, I love you, but, you weren’t a great player.”

When the Guardian reached out to two-time WNBA champion coach Michael Cooper for his thoughts on the greatest trash talkers in league history, he was quick to mention Cynthia Cooper (unrelated). A two-time MVP and four-time champ with the 1990s Houston Comets, Cynthia was a marvel on the floor. But she didn’t go about her business silently, often making her feelings known to Michael’s LA Sparks in the playoffs. “We were playing them for their second title and I was an assistant coach,” Michael says. “She walked by me during a timeout and said, ‘Coop, we beating y’all like the Celtics did in 8’84.’ I couldn’t help but laugh. She was a shit talker!”

Teresa Weatherspoon

Speaking of those 1990s Comets, one of their former players, Fran Harris, was quick to note Weatherspoon’s trash talking ability. Of course, Weatherspoon hit perhaps the biggest shot in WNBA history (against the 1999 Comets). But even before that, the two-time Defensive Player of the Year filled arenas with her biting smack talk, not unlike another former DPOY, Gary Payton.

TechnologyTab.title: AI giant Anthropic woos potential investors ahead of stock market debut
TechnologyTab.text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic has been drumming up support for its expected stock market listing as it seeks to reassure investors of its profit-making potential.

Anthropic revenue surged by 45% to $16.8bn (£12.7bn) in the three months to the end of September, the BBC understands.

In common with other AI firms, it is seeking to position itself as being able to generate huge profits despite spending billions on tech.

It also emphasised safety at its event after warnings by current and former researchers of serious and even existential risks to humanity posed by AI.

Anthropic's revenue has risen in successive quarters this year, from $4.7bn in the first three months to $11.6bn the following period.

The company also told investors during the event at its headquarters in San Francisco that it had made a third quarter profit on an adjusted basis, an accounting method which ignores non-recurring costs.

Investors reportedly left the Anthropic investor event optimistic about the company's rapid revenue growth and path to profitability.

Alongside concerns about profit generation, there have also been fears about the safety of AI models.

Anthropic has been vocal about AI's risks, with its chief executive Dario Amodei calling on the pace of development to slow down.

In September one of its researchers warned of a greater than 10% chance that AI could "kill all humans" within the next decade, and a former researcher said people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity.

The firm itself said in September it had identified and disrupted attempts to use its AI model for "malicious activity" which could support the development of biological weapons.

However, US President Donald Trump has said researchers have been "bringing up things that won't happen" and that in a race between the US and China to develop the technology, "whoever wins AI, wins".

Rival tech firm OpenAI has also warned about safety, with its chief executive Sam Altman saying in September that his company will not go public this year as it addresses concerns.

The ChatGPT-developer is also eyeing a bumper stock market listing, which is expected to value the firm at more than $1tn.

TechnologyTab.title: Netflix to shed 1,000 jobs in steepest cuts since 2022
TechnologyTab.text:
Netflix has said it will cut 1,000 jobs globally as the streaming giant faces competition from rivals.

The cuts - the steepest since 2022 - will mainly affect its human resources, legal, product and technology teams and equates to around 6% of its total workforce.

Last month, Netflix 's co-chief executive, Ted Sarandos, told the Bloomberg Screentime summit that the company was "not growing as fast as I want us to".

The streaming industry is going through a period of consolidation following Paramount's $110bn (£83.6bn) merger with Warner Bros, the owner of HBO, while free platforms such as YouTube and TikTok continue to attract viewers.

In an email to staff, Sarandos and co-chief executive Greg Peters said Netflix would "continue to invest aggressively in high-impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation".

Netflix had come close to its own deal with Warner Bros but was outbid in the end by Paramount.

Commenting on the "organisational changes", Sarandos and Peters said: "Our mission - to entertain the world - is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritise our people and resources."

Managers will tell employees whether their job has been cut "soon".

TechnologyTab.title: Toilet paper and secret recorders: What we know about the arrest of the Saudi OpenAI engineer
TechnologyTab.text:
A Saudi national who worked for OpenAI appeared in court this week for allegedly planting a secret recording device behind a TV in one of the tech giant's meeting rooms.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer, was arrested by the FBI and charged with using or attempting to use a device "to intercept oral communications".

As yet, it is not clear what he was planning to do with the recordings.

But, here's we do know so far.

The engineer asked AI to help him listen in to discussions about AI, according to an official complaint (the document filed in court).

Between 17 August and 16 September, Alfozan had reportedly asked a productivity AI assistant several questions about meeting rooms and their availability.

Some detailed in the complaint include "how about external partners, where would they usually meet with OpenAI at" and "can you list today's meeting in this room".

The complaint also claimed that in September, Alfozan used a chatbot associated with his spouse to ask how to build and install a recording device and how to access it remotely.

Alfozan had worked at the firm for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant a recorder.

The room where the device was found was regularly used to hold meetings to discuss "highly confidential technical, commercial and strategic information" as well as OpenAI's "government engagements and commercial relationships", the complaint stated.

Alfozan had no authority to access or be involved with meetings in the room, the complaint states.

But CCTV footage recorded him near the conference room on eight separate occasions in September.

On 30 September, OpenAI staff discovered a "surreptitious audio recording device" behind a television - which had been wrapped in toilet paper.

A camera was placed in the conference room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering the room and appeared to look behind the television where the device had been inserted.

The complaint also stated that same day he allegedly left an unattended bag in a different room.

When security personnel opened it, it was found to contain "another recording device" similar to the one discovered, as well as Alfozan's wallet and ID.

In a post on X, external, OpenAI wrote it had used its own AI models to "understand the device and where it had come from".

It also said: "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data."

TechnologyTab.title: GTA 6: Release date, how much it is and everything you need to know
TechnologyTab.text:
Rockstar has released a new launch trailer for Grand Theft Auto VI, revealing more details about what is set to be the biggest game of the year.

GTA 6 became available to pre-order at midnight on 25 June in the UK and elsewhere around the world, after Rockstar revealed the game's pre-sales launch date and cover art in mid-June.

Analysts believe Rockstar's action adventure could become the most expensive game ever made, with estimates, external putting development costs at more than $1bn (£866m).

Here's what we do and don't know about GTA 6 so far.

The new launch trailer, external again confirmed GTA 6 will be released on 19 November.

Suggesting no further delays to its release, the video gave fans a glimpse into the missions that protagonists Jason and Lucia will take part in.

It also featured a new song from French electronic music artists Justice, who were revealed to be the game's original score composers.

The game has been previously delayed twice, from autumn 2025 and May 2026.

In a statement when the second delay was announced, Rockstar said it needed extra months to finish the game with the level of polish fans had come to "expect and deserve".

Rockstar said players who pre-order will be able to begin pre-loading it on their consoles on 12 November to ensure they are able to play at launch.

The sixth game in the main series will be released on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X and S.

There's no news on when a PC version will be released - it's also currently unknown whether it will come to Nintendo Switch 2.

The game will cost £69.99 in the UK and $79.99 in the US - with an ultimate edition, featuring extra vehicles and weapons, priced at £89.99 and $99.99, respectively.

Physical copies of the game will contain a code for a digital download for the game inside a box, rather than a disc.

Rockstar has not yet confirmed whether an updated online mode will be released as soon as GTA 6 launches.

The game's PlayStation Store listing currently states "Grand Theft Auto VI is a single-player experience" - implying there will be no online mode at launch. But given GTA Online's success, external, it will likely exist at some point.

How any future age verification legislation in the UK around social media and particularly messaging in gaming could therefore affect it, if at all, is still unknown.

GTA 6 will feature its first ever playable female protagonist in a 3D setting - Lucia - alongside her partner in life and crime, Jason, as a second playable character.

From what we've seen in two gameplay trailers and Netflix's extended look, the story will follow the pair in a Bonnie and Clyde-esque adventure through the seedy underbelly of America after an "easy score goes wrong, external".

Like other GTA games before it, the sixth chapter is set in a fictional US state - this time in Leonida, which is Rockstar's version of Florida.

Fans of previous games will be excited to hear that Vice City, which is inspired by Miami, will return, featuring as the main city within the state.

GTA 6's cover art revealed by Rockstar on 18 June made several nods to the setting with alligators and flamingos.

It's no secret that GTA 6 has been a few years in the making.

The franchise's last instalment, GTA 5, was released in September 2013 - and quickly became one of the best-selling games of all time.

It's unclear whether Rockstar has been working on the sixth instalment for all of that time, however, as in 2018 it also released another huge sequel - Red Dead Redemption 2.

Rockstar confirmed for the first time that it was working on a sixth game in the series in February 2022.

The rising cost of development and immense pressure to live up to the series' hype are all contributing factors as to why gamers have had to wait so long for the game's release.

Several months later, footage and images leaked after teenage hackers targeted the company.

It has also seen some issues since, including accusations of "union-busting" by sacked workers at Rockstar North, its Edinburgh HQ, where developers have been racing to get GTA 6 ready for release in November.

To put it simply, the GTA franchise is one of the biggest and most profitable entertainment properties in history.

GTA 5 has sold nearly 230 million copies, making it one of the best-selling games of all time - which has generated billions of dollars in revenue for Rockstar.

The game's sandbox gameplay, where players can explore vast open worlds with considerable freedom - sometimes controversially - has seen it be continuously lauded as the ultimate expression for what the interactive medium can do.

Freelance video games journalist Vic Hood said each entry in the series "continued to push technical and gameplay boundaries", with GTA Online helping to "pioneer the live service model as we know it".

She added that the games were also "extremely culturally relevant" too.

"Rockstar has always had its finger on the pulse of music, entertainment, societal, political, celebrity, and online culture trends, and they've never shied away from satirising these things in GTA games," she said.

British gaming entrepreneur Sir Ian Livingstone told the BBC's Today programme that the series, originally developed in Scotland, was "bigger than any film or song" and an "incredible achievement in interactive software".

Speculation as to how a sixth game can top even the gigantic heights of its predecessor has meant that any latest news, no matter how small, has been met with a flurry of hype and excitement.

Both of GTA 6's previous gameplay trailers currently have a total of roughly 447 million views combined.

TechnologyTab.title: 'I applied for 200 jobs' - How 'spray and pray' AI job applications can backfire
TechnologyTab.text:
Would you use AI to help you write a CV or cover letter? How about during an online assessment or video interview for a job?

We are increasingly using the technology to help us with job applications, graduates, external and recruiters say, with many employers happy for us to do so within reason.

But when does it cross a line from being acceptable to unethical, or even cheating?

Tom, 22, from Maidstone graduated last year with a geography degree and says he applied for over 200 jobs before finally landing a role last month as a restaurant manager.

He says the process was "exhausting" and "demoralising", with employers often not even getting back to him, and he wouldn't have got through it without some help from AI.

"Employers want you to put your absolute best into the application, but if I'm applying for 10 to 20 jobs in a day, the reality is you can't do that."

While Tom says he never used the technology in an assessment or interview, he did use it to help him with cover letters and CVs or to find the right "buzz words" that early stage screening in a recruitment process will pick up on.

He also thinks it's "hypocritical" for companies to ask candidates not to use AI when some are using it themselves to screen candidates.

"That's where it feels like a weird tightrope. You can't use AI too much because otherwise you're not human. But if you don't write like an AI, you may get skipped by the AI screening."

This summer, the Institute of Student Employers (ISE) surveyed 155 of the UK's biggest graduate employers and found they were becoming "more accepting" of candidates using AI "at some stages of the recruitment process".

According to the trade group, the most commonly accepted use was writing cover letters or CVs, followed by completing online application questions.

However, it also found 92% of employers had encountered or suspected AI "misconduct" in the job selection process - up from 85% last year. Most commonly this included using AI as a real-time assistant during online video interviews or to complete online assessments.

On top of this, the tech is helping candidates write multiple applications at the same time - something known in the industry as "spray and pray". Stephen Isherwood, joint chief executive of the ISE, says it is "driving up the competition and pressure on students" in an already competitive graduate recruitment market.

Hollie Moody, head of early careers recruitment at energy giant EDF, says she doesn't blame graduates for using AI in applications given how "brutal" the jobs market is right now. But she does think it's becoming a problem.

EDF opened its graduate recruitment scheme three weeks ago, but decided to close it early after receiving 12,000 applications - a 10% increase on last year.

Moody says AI almost certainly contributed to this, adding that the tech is being used "a lot more freely" in the actual selection process.

"What we don't have is a level playing field, because what you'll find is that some candidates will absolutely use AI throughout the whole process, and other candidates won't."

Like many firms, EDF now issues guidance on the appropriate use of AI in job applications, and is trying to make its recruitment process as "AI-proof" as possible.

It only reads CVs in the later stages of the hiring process and uses skills and behaviour-based online assessments and video interviews to better assess candidates.

But Moody says some applicants still try to bend the rules, particularly in video interviews.

"A lot of the answers [we hear] are the same. Or people might pause whilst they wait for AI to come back to them with an answer. It's almost like people are reading a script."

One recently employed trainee accountant, who didn't want us to use his real name, told the BBC he'd applied for 50 graduate jobs and used AI in every application. But he says it was only for researching roles, tidying up his CV and generating mock practise questions for video interviews.

While he says he would never use the tech to cheat on assessments he knows people who would.

"I know people who have applied for 100 jobs and after a while they become desperate. If they see everyone else is using AI, they think how can I compete?"

According to the ISE, the graduate market has stabilised after a sharp fall last year but remains tough. Graduate roles currently attract an average of 141 applications each, it says.

And while only 16% of employers it surveyed are using AI in the recruitment process, 29% plan to introduce it within the next year.

Hollie Moody says EDF does not currently use AI in its recruitment process but may have to in future.

For her, the use of AI in job applications remains a "moral dilemma" that employers and candidates will continue to grapple with. But she stresses it cannot replace what her firm is looking for in new recruits.

"It's about authenticity, but also personality. We want diversity of thought in the business."

TechnologyTab.title: How long will humans be needed for translation?
TechnologyTab.text:
"Il pleut des cordes," say the French when it's raining hard.

"It's raining ropes," is the direct translation. It's the kind of idiom which can trip up an AI translator.

"You can imagine the dilemma this throws AI into," says François Yvon, a research director specialised in automatic translation with the French National Centre for Scientific Research CNRS.

He says a well-trained system will know that ropes are not literally falling from the sky and use the English phrase "it's raining cats and dogs".

"But is it going to find the equivalent when it's translating into Indonesian?" asks Yvon.

A comment on the weather is pretty low-risk, but more and more translation is being done by machines, and on topics with higher stakes than the weather.

In April, Google said people are now translating, external one trillion words a month with Google Translate.

That doesn't count the others: DeepL, Microsoft, Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini, not to mention made-to-measure corporate translation systems.

Direct sales of machine translation, external (i.e. outside general AI subscriptions) were worth an estimated $1.4bn (£1bn) last year.

"For plenty of use cases, raw AI translation is now the right call: multiplying your costs by 100 to catch the last few percent of errors isn't rational if you're translating internal documents or product listings," says Jonathan Zimmerman, founder of OKA (Open Knowledge Association), a Swiss non-profit that translates Wikipedia articles into other languages.

"For an encyclopedia it's different. Wikipedia runs on trust. A wrong fact can sit there for years and get cited by journalists and AI systems," he says.

With more than 10,000 published pieces, mostly into Spanish, Portuguese and English, OKA is, Zimmerman says, the single largest contributor of translated articles to the collaborative online encyclopedia.

Which is something it absolutely could not have become without AI.

"Translating 10,000 articles the traditional way would cost millions. In our process, the AI produces the draft, then a human translator checks every sentence," he explains.

But that human input is required less and less.

"The machine output is now good enough that skipping the human entirely has become a serious option, and a real temptation across the industry. Two or three years ago, with tools like DeepL, our translators still rewrote a good chunk of every draft.

"Today the prose often doesn't need fixing at all. So, the question is no longer whether AI translation is good, it clearly is, but whether it's good enough to remove the human," says Zimmerman.

Not yet, translators argue.

Ariella Baltié is a translator and legal expert specialised in translating court documents from English into French.

She was contacted recently by someone who'd already translated his documents with AI, asking her to check them.

"There were two major errors right at the beginning," she said.

The AI had translated "Le demandeur" (the plaintiff) as "the requester". "Totally awkward for legal papers," says Baltié.

When the AI saw "Madame X, épouse Y" (Ms X, wife of Y'), it came up with "Ms X marries Y".

In other words, it mistook a noun for a verb, completely losing the meaning of the phrase.

The consequences of mistranslation in the legal sphere can be serious. In the US, for example, errors in machine-translated asylum applications have led to delays in the release of detainees.

Accuracy is a matter of life and death in the medical field.

"The units for dosages and blood tests often include Greek letters," says Carol Bereuter, who is a specialist in medical translations.

She came across one automatically-translated text that had translated the greek letter μ as milli (one thousandth) instead of micro (one millionth).

"That's a serious error. If you give someone a milligram when it's meant to be a microgram, you are giving them a thousand times the dose," points out Bereuter.

She also makes the point that, as AI translators have got better, catching errors has got more difficult.

"Whereas in the past, with things like Google Translate, the sentence would jump out at you because there'd be a grammatical error or it would sound clunky, today it sounds perfectly legitimate. It sounds fluid. It sounds natural. So the errors are a lot harder to spot."

"If it's something that will bear your signature, there's a risk for your reputation. And if decisions are going to be taken on the basis of a translation concerning a medical procedure, a contract you might sign or a major purchase you might make, the risk is even greater," warns François Yvon.

Even sentences that seem quite clear to a human can trip up an AI service, he says.

"When you have words with different meanings, it's usually very clear for a human which one applies because they understand the context, but when a machine translator comes across the sentence 'translate into Polish', for example, it is quite capable of deciding it must be all about shoe cream, says Yvon.

Context is often crucial. If an AI translator hasn't grasped that we're talking about a football match it is liable to mis-translate "taking a corner".

Last year OKA ran a study, funded by Wikimedia. It studied 119 articles, 10 language pairs and more than 1,000 hours of translator work.

"27% of the AI-generated text still got corrected before publication. Three quarters of those corrections were errors the AI introduced, and 5 to 6% of errors changed the meaning of the original text," says Zimmerman.

Eradicating those errors is likely to be challenging.

"As things stand, I think the fundamental way these systems function makes it quite hard to imagine how they could become 100% reliable," says François Yvon.

This is because probability is a crucial part of the way AI translates each word rather than another and what is probably correct is not the same as what is correct. Especially in the realm of something as subtle and surprising as language.

He thinks a new generation of tech will be an improvement.

"We will see translation systems that are increasingly capable of evaluating what they do and correcting themselves using different AI tools simultaneously: one to do the translation, a second to criticize it and a third to produce a new version, for example."

But perhaps the big moment will be when AI can show doubt.

"The real breakthrough won't come until these systems are not merely capable of translating but also of telling us when they're not sure," Yvon says.
